title: Tria capita ex opere quodam majori inedito de theoria lunae

deep.reconstruction:
Purpose: fit the constants of the lunar theory (mean longitude, anomaly, node, eccentricity) to observed geocentric positions of the Moon. Lunar eclipses are chosen because they are free of parallax. The previous page explains that the difficulty is to extract the instant of opposition from the observed contact times.

§3 sets up a spherical model. A great circle ☊Ss is the ecliptic and a great circle ☊Ll is the lunar orbit, meeting at the node ☊. At first contact the shadow centre (the anti-solar point) is at S and the Moon's centre at L. At last contact they are at s and l. Because the umbra's and the Moon's apparent radii are taken as constant during the eclipse, SL = sl. Euler also makes three simplifications:
- the node is held fixed, and all motions are measured relative to it;
- the motions are uniform over a few hours;
- inequalities of a few arc-minutes over that interval are neglected.

§4 fixes the contact distances. With umbral radius α = π_moon + π_sun − s_sun and lunar radius β, first and last contact give SL = sl = α + β. Internal contacts (immersion and emersion in a total eclipse) give SL = sl = α − β. Only the equality is needed, so α and β themselves need not be known.

§5 introduces the motions. Let the duration be h hours, and the hourly motions be m (Sun), n (Moon) and k (node, retrograde). Measured from the node:
- Ss = h(m + k) and Ll = h(n + k);
- after t hours, Sσ = (m + k)t and Lλ = (n + k)t.

§6 changes the target instant. True opposition would be the moment when σλ is perpendicular to the ecliptic, which would then require reducing the Moon's place to the ecliptic. Euler instead seeks the moment when ☊σ = ☊λ, i.e. when the Moon's longitude counted along its own orbit from the node equals the longitude of the shadow centre. At that moment the solar theory directly gives the Moon's orbital longitude, which is exactly what the lunar tables tabulate, so no reduction to the ecliptic is needed.

The next page completes the method. Put x = ☊σ = ☊λ and inclination ρ. The spherical cosine rule in triangles ☊SL and ☊sl, together with SL = sl, yields (1 + cos ρ)[cos(n−m)t − cos(n−m)(h−t)] = (1 − cos ρ)[cos(2x + (m+n+2k)(h−t)) − cos(2x − (m+n+2k)t)]. This equation is to be solved for t (and x).
errors: Notation is inconsistent within §5: Ss = h(m''+k'') but Sσ = (m+k)t''. The seconds mark migrates from the rates to the product; this is cosmetic.

The umbral radius α = π_moon + π_sun − s_sun omits the atmospheric enlargement of the shadow that was known in Euler's time. It is harmless here because only SL = sl is used, provided the enlargement is constant during the eclipse.

Using n + k as the Moon's rate along its orbit relative to the node treats the ecliptic-longitude rate and the orbital rate as interchangeable. The difference is of order (1 − cos i), which is negligible.

ideas.what: Using lunar eclipse contact times, which are parallax-free and symmetric (first/last or immersion/emersion), to determine the Moon's true place for fitting the constants of a lunar theory
ideas.modern_name: Determination of the time of opposition / middle of eclipse from contact timings
ideas.usually_credited_to: Ancient practice (Hipparchus, Ptolemy); refined by early-modern astronomers
ideas.where_published: Possibly related material in Euler's lunar theories (E187 Theoria motus lunae 1753; E418 Theoria motuum lunae 1772); unsure

ideas.what: Choosing the instant of equal node-distances (☊σ = ☊λ) instead of true opposition, so the Moon's orbital longitude is obtained directly without reduction to the ecliptic
ideas.modern_name: Use of argument of latitude / orbital longitude; avoiding 'reductio ad eclipticam'
ideas.usually_credited_to: unsure; a standard convenience in table-making

ideas.what: Exact spherical-trigonometric condition SL = sl, with the node and the motions relative to the node as unknowns
ideas.modern_name: Spherical cosine rule applied to eclipse geometry

deep.surprise_reason: A careful but standard reduction of eclipse observations. The only slightly distinctive touch is targeting the equal-node-distance instant rather than true opposition, which is a practical convenience rather than a new result.
transcription_corrections: §3: the lunar orbit is 'circulus ☊Ll' (the edge of the scan is cut off); '☊L[?]' should read ☊Ll.
§3, line 3: the ending is 'centrum lunae vero in l' (the scan shows 'vero in l').
§4: 'etiamsi ipsi arcus SL et sl non sint cogniti' is confirmed.
§5: the image has 'Sin autem elapsis ab initio' as in the transcription; the text is consistent.
